senses.definition: Using far more words than the point needs. It is a judgement about the words, not the content, so something can be entirely correct and still be verbose, which is what makes it a chore to read.
senses.caution: It criticises the writer, not only the writing, and it stings more than long or dense. Said out loud about someone's answer while others are listening it is close to rude; keep it for drafts, for logs, and for your own work. It also has a flat, non-insulting life in engineering, where verbose output or verbose logging just means detailed, so in a mixed room make clear which of the two you mean.
senses.example: It is accurate, but it is verbose. The committee will read the opening paragraph and stop.

cues.text: A colleague's weekly update runs to four paragraphs where two lines would do, and you are giving them the feedback privately.
You reread your own memo before sending it and notice it takes half a page to reach the ask.
A friend forwards you the terms of a phone contract that says almost nothing across two thousand words.
You gave up on a novel a hundred pages in because every scene took three pages to move an inch.

distractors: Written in unnecessarily technical language, so that a general reader stalls on the vocabulary rather than the argument.
Delivered so fast that nobody can follow it, the argument fine on the page and gone by the time you look up from your notes.

Deliberately vague so as to avoid committing to anything, phrased so that either outcome can afterwards be read as the one that was meant. The evasion is the point of it, and it can be managed in very few words.

Formal to the point of coldness, correct in every particular and offering the reader nothing at all to hold on to. It is a complaint about the temperature of the writing rather than about how much of it there is.

Full of confident claims with nothing standing behind any of them, so that the register stays certain and the evidence never arrives. What is wrong is the gap between the assurance and the support, which a short paragraph manages as easily as a long one.
